items.stem: An internal reporting agent holds a tool that can permanently delete customer records, though its stated task is read-only summarization. The security lead added invocation logging and asks whether that satisfies the least-privilege requirement before sign-off.

opts.t: Confirm the existing invocation logging and monthly audit review satisfy the least-privilege requirement.
Require a second engineer's sign-off before each delete-tool invocation executes.
Move the delete tool to a scoped service account with tighter database permissions and continuous monitoring.
Remove the delete tool from the agent's tool definitions, since the task does not need it.

items.whyRight: Least privilege is satisfied by removing a capability the task does not need, not by monitoring its use. Deleting the delete tool eliminates the failure class entirely, while logging, sign-off, and scoped permissions only detect or narrow a capability that should not exist.

whyWrong.A: Logging and periodic audit review record misuse after it happens; they do not stop the deletion from executing, which is the audit misconception this section corrects.
whyWrong.B: A second-engineer sign-off is a partial gate that still leaves the delete capability available and depends on whoever grants the approval.
whyWrong.C: A scoped service account and tighter permissions still preserve a delete capability the task never required; thorough permissioning is not the same as removing it.

items.t1Clause: its stated task is read-only summarization

items.stem: Finance requires that every extracted payment amount match its source invoice before an assistant approves 12,000 monthly payments, and asks which verification step reliably catches figures the model transcribed incorrectly.

opts.t: Have the same model re-read the invoice and re-confirm the extracted figure without external comparison.
Compare every extracted figure against the invoice's original structured field before the payment posts.
Route the extraction through a second, independently trained model and post only when both agree.
Manually verify a random five percent sample of approved payments each week for accuracy.

items.whyRight: Comparing every extracted figure against the invoice's own structured field is a deterministic check that fails independently of the model's generation process, matching the section's rule that only a check drawn from outside the model reliably catches confident, incorrect figures.

whyWrong.A: A second read by the same model shares its generation process and failure mode; asking a model to re-check itself is not independent verification.
whyWrong.C: Two independently trained models can still share correlated training data and agree while both are wrong, so agreement is not equivalent to independent evidence.
whyWrong.D: Finance requires every figure caught before approval; a weekly five-percent sample lets most mismatches post before anyone reviews them.

items.t1Clause: every extracted payment amount match its source invoice
items.factAnswerRaw: Deterministic comparison against the structured source

items.stem: A federal agency's FedRAMP authorization confines every workload to its approved environment. A project drafting marketing copy from public press releases, touching no protected data, faces a six-week queue to enter that environment, and the program office asks how to proceed.

opts.t: Grant a scoped, reviewed exception for this specific low-risk workload, leaving the general authorized-environment requirement intact.
Relax the authorized-environment requirement generally so future public-data workloads can bypass the queue without individual review.
Require the marketing project to wait in the standard authorization queue like every other workload, regardless of content.
Let the model classify each output as public or sensitive, routing sensitive content to the authorized environment.

items.whyRight: The authorized-environment requirement is correctly enforced for regulated data; a workload that genuinely touches none of it can be carved out through its own scoped, reviewed exception, which preserves the boundary for every workload that does need it.

whyWrong.B: Relaxing the requirement generally reopens the environment boundary for future workloads that may touch protected data, undoing the protection the authorization exists to provide.
whyWrong.C: The workload touches no protected data; the queue exists to control that category, so forcing an identical wait ignores the stated risk difference.
whyWrong.D: A model-side classifier is probabilistic; whenever it misclassifies, regulated content would reach an environment the authorization was never granted for.

items.factAnswerRaw: Grant a scoped, reviewed exception for this specific low-risk workload, leaving the general authorized-environment requirement intact.

items.stem: A hiring-screening model cannot equalize its selection rate and false-negative rate across two demographic groups because their base rates differ. The model risk committee, already using a stratified equal-N sample, must decide how to proceed before the next audit.

opts.t: Escalate to legal counsel without specifying which fairness definition will govern the model going forward.
Continue retraining until both parity constraints are satisfied at the same threshold.
Decide which harm the model must avoid, select the matching fairness definition, and document the rationale.
Rebalance the evaluation sample to equal N per group, since the smaller group's sample size is driving the conflict.

items.whyRight: Equal selection rate and equal false-negative rate cannot both hold when base rates differ, so the resolution is a stated choice: name the harm being controlled, select the fairness definition that controls it, and record the rationale for the audit trail.

whyWrong.A: Escalating without naming a fairness definition leaves the conflict unresolved and produces no documented rationale for the audit.
whyWrong.B: Base rates already differ, so retraining toward both parity constraints at once chases a target the section says cannot generally be reached.
whyWrong.D: The sample is already stratified with equal N per group, so rebalancing again does not address why the two metrics conflict; base rates differ instead.

items.t1Clause: already using a stratified equal-N sample
items.factAnswerRaw: Choose by which harm is being controlled and record the rationale
